American cinema. The body of films produced in the United States, and especially the industrial and artistic dominance of Hollywood from the nineteen twenties through the present. American films shaped global visual language, narrative conventions, and entertainment itself, exporting American values, optimism, and mythology to the world. Hollywood became synonymous with cinema as an art form and an industry, creating distinctive genres and star systems that defined popular culture.

The studio system, roughly from the nineteen twenties through the nineteen fifties, consolidated production under a few major studios—MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., Fox, and RKO. They controlled actors, directors, screenwriters, and distribution, creating a vertically integrated industrial machine.

The Golden Age of cinema in the nineteen thirties and forties produced classics of screwball comedy, detective fiction, westerns, and melodrama. These films established the narrative and visual conventions still taught and imitated.

American cinema developed a distinctive optimism centered on the American dream, the everyman hero, and belief in individual agency and democracy, especially in films by Frank Capra. Genre became central to American filmmaking—westerns, musicals, film noir, comedy, war films—each with recognizable visual and narrative codes that audiences came to expect.

The star system created a culture of celebrity. Actors like James Stewart, Humphrey Bogart, and Audrey Hepburn became mythic figures whose personas shaped the roles they played.

American cinema's influence is global. It set technical standards, narrative structures, and thematic preoccupations that other film industries adopted, adapted, or rebelled against.

Post-war shifts from the nineteen fifties onward saw the rise of television, the decline of the studio system, and the emergence of director-driven, more adult-oriented cinema.
